title: The Stampede at 6 AM

post.author: u/first_bell_astrid
post.title: I open the doors at a department store. Two sale mornings running, by 6:00:01 every price board in the building had gone dark.

blocks.text: I ring the first bell at Brackwater's on Corran Street, a department store since 1909: six brass doors, and on sale mornings a crowd outside from four. This summer's refit gave us new tills and a price board above every rail. Every till, board and price checker asks the price service for a price, and each open door's crowd brings 100 of those lookups a second. The service keeps the 50 sale prices in a cache, 10 minutes each. On a miss it asks the stockroom database to rebuild the price: find the item, apply the sale, count the stock. Lucan, our IT man, says the stockroom works on 50 rebuilds at once, half a second each, 100 a second. Give it more and it shares its time, and every rebuild slows. A till waits 2 seconds, then gives up.
Monday was the first sale since the refit, and the cache was empty. At 6:00 I rang the bell and opened all six doors. Lucan's log:

06:00:00  bell. doors 1-6 open   lookups 600/s
06:00:01  boards lit 0 of 50   stockroom asked 600/s
06:00:02  tills giving up: no price in 2 s
06:00:10  stockroom: 6,000 rebuilds in progress, 0 done

The whole crowd stopped under dark boards, and nobody spoke. At 6:04 a doorman in the old grey livery walked them back out into the street, and Lucan restarted the stockroom. Then the doorman opened door 1, only door 1, and in under a second every board was lit. Ten seconds later he opened door 2, then door 3. Lucan says we haven't had a doorman since 1987.
The cameras show the crowd turning round at once. They don't show what turned it.

On Tuesday Lucan added a warm-up: at 5:50 a script asks for all 50 prices, so they're in the cache before the bell. At 6:00 every board was lit. Half a second later they all went dark in the same instant, and the store froze again. The doorman was already at door 1. Afterwards we found this behind the loading bay, in a bin from the refit:

blocks.title: BRACKWATER'S, DOOR 1
items: WHEN THE DOORS OPEN AT 6 AM,
LET THEM IN A FEW AT A TIME.

blocks.text: Lucan says the plate is superstition and the prices are maths. What should he change before Wednesday?

blocks.label: lucan_dashboard_monday_060010.png

diagram.aria: Lucan's dashboard at 6:00:10 on Monday. The tills and boards send 600 lookups a second to the price service, which looks in the price cache first. The cache is empty, 0 of 50 prices, so none are hits, and all 600 a second go to the stockroom database, which works on 50 rebuilds at once at full speed, half a second each. It has 6,000 rebuilds in progress and has finished none. Tills are giving up at 600 a second.

blocks.caption: Lucan's dashboard at 6:00:10 on Monday, redrawn. 600 lookups a second reach the price service. The cache is empty, so every one is a miss and asks the stockroom for a rebuild: 600 a second, for only 50 prices. The stockroom has 6,000 rebuilds in progress, each slowed to a crawl, and hasn't finished one. Every till gives up after 2 seconds, 600 a second.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Three words for what you saw, then some questions. A thundering herd is many clients doing the same thing at the same moment: six doors, one bell. A cache stampede, also called a dogpile, is what a herd does to a cache: a price is missing, every lookup for it misses together, and each one asks the stockroom to rebuild the same price. And a cache that's empty, after a refit, a restart or a deploy, is cold: its hit ratio is 0, so for a while every lookup is a rebuild. Now look at Lucan's log. 6,000 rebuilds in progress for 50 prices: how many times was each price being rebuilt? Why did none of them finish, when one rebuild takes half a second? Why did Tuesday's warm cache go dark in the same second as Monday's empty one? And what did one open door do that six couldn't?

replies.author: u/first_bell_astrid
replies.text: Lucan did the sums. 120 times each, in ten seconds. Then he asked me again who the doorman was.

comments.author: u/dogpile_dunstan
comments.text: Every one of Monday's misses asked for a price another till had already asked for. Make the misses for one price share one rebuild: the first miss asks the stockroom, and the rest wait for its answer. That's request coalescing, also called single flight, and Go even has a package for it, singleflight, that does it inside one program. Across many servers the shared cache has to help: a lock on the key, so only one server rebuilds it, or what Facebook's memcache calls leases. On a miss, the cache gives one client a token that lets it put the value back, and tells the others to wait a moment and ask again. One catch. Everyone waiting now rides on one rebuild, so if it hangs, they all hang. Give it a timeout too.

comments.author: u/stale_shelf_wanjiru
comments.text: For a price that has only just run out there's a gentler trick: keep the old price a little longer and hand it out at once, while one lookup fetches the new one in the background. HTTP caches call it stale-while-revalidate. We allow up to a minute past the TTL, so a board shows a price a few seconds old instead of going dark. It isn't the serve-stale a DNS resolver falls back on when the nameserver is down: this is on purpose, every time a price runs out. And it does nothing for a cold cache. There's nothing old to hand out.

comments.author: u/cold_open_aurelio
comments.text: Warming the cache before the doors open is right. It's why Tuesday got half a second of lit boards that Monday never had. The catch is how Lucan did it: one script, all 50 prices in the same half second, every one for exactly 10 minutes. Keys that go in together with the same TTL run out together. We give every key a small random extra on its TTL, a couple of minutes at most, so they run out one or two at a time instead of all at once. That's jitter, the same trick you use on retry waits, moved to the expiry.

replies.author: u/first_bell_astrid
replies.text: Lucan says 5:50:00.5 plus ten minutes is 6:00:00.5. He's checked it nine times, and every time he says it out loud, the lights in the stockroom flicker.

reply.prompt: Wednesday is the third sale morning. What should Lucan change before 6 AM? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep Lucan's warm-up and give every price a 24-hour TTL, so not one price runs out while the doors are open.
options.part2: Lucan set the TTL to 24 hours on Tuesday night. At 5:50 on Wednesday the warm-up put the 50 prices in, and at 6:00 I opened all six doors. Every board was lit, and not one price ran out all morning. At 9:00 Perpetua in pricing marked the winter coats down from 180 to 120, and the boards went on saying 180. At 11:40 Lucan deployed a fix, and the deploy restarted the price cache. It came back empty with the whole crowd inside: 600 lookups a second, every one a miss, every one a rebuild. By 11:40:10 the stockroom had 6,000 rebuilds in progress and had finished none. When I got down to the floor, the crowd was already filing out into the street, quietly, toward a man in grey at door 1.
options.senior: A long TTL hides the herd at 6:00, but the cache still empties: on a deploy, a restart or a failed node. When it does, the whole crowd is inside, every lookup is a rebuild, and nothing protects the stockroom. Meanwhile every price can be a day out of date. Fix the herd itself: rebuild each key once, spread the expiries, and after every restart warm the cache and let traffic in gradually, not only at the bell.

options.text: Keep the warm-up, add a random 0 to 2 minutes to each TTL, turn on coalescing, and open one door every 10 seconds.
options.part2: Lucan changed all three on Tuesday night. At 5:50 on Wednesday the warm-up put the 50 prices in, each for 10 minutes plus its own random extra of up to 2. At 6:00 I rang the bell and opened door 1, then another every 10 seconds, and all six were open by 6:00:50. Between 6:00:00.5 and 6:02:00.5 the prices ran out one or two at a time, and each came back in under a second after a single rebuild: 50 rebuilds in two minutes, never more than 2 at once. At 11:40 Lucan deployed a fix and the price cache came back empty with the store full. 600 lookups a second missed together, but the stockroom got one rebuild per price, and half a second later every board was lit. Nobody on the floor looked up. When I locked door 1 that evening, the brass plate was back on it, polished. Lucan says he didn't put it there.
options.senior: Each fix covers a different moment the cache can't answer. The warm-up covers the bell. Jitter stops prices that went in together from running out together. Coalescing caps every herd at one rebuild per price, even the deploy nobody planned for. And opening one door at a time keeps the first misses inside what the stockroom can rebuild. Serving the old price while one lookup refreshes would hide even the half-second blinks, and with more than one price server, coalescing needs a lock or a lease in the external cache to stay one rebuild per price.

options.text: Open one door every 10 seconds, as the brass plate says, and leave the warm-up and the price service as they are.
options.verdict: Trade-off: the doors are safe, the cache isn't
options.part2: On Wednesday the warm-up ran at 5:50 and I opened door 1 at 6:00. At 6:00:00.5 every warmed price ran out at once, but with one door open the stockroom rebuilt them one each, and every board was lit again by 6:00:01.4. I opened a door every 10 seconds. By 6:00:50 all six were open and every board was lit. At 6:10:01 every price ran out again within half a second, because they had all gone back in within half a second, and this time the whole crowd was inside. 600 lookups a second, every one a miss, and not one price came back. The tills gave up two seconds later. I went to find the doorman. He was at door 1, holding it shut, shaking his head.
options.senior: The brass plate's rule protects the moment traffic arrives: one door's 100 lookups a second rebuild 50 prices without ever giving the stockroom more than its 50 at once. It does nothing about the cache's own herds. Prices that go in together run out together, and by then every door is open. Opening slowly is for the bell; jitter and coalescing are for every moment after it when the cache forgets.

options.text: Turn on coalescing, so each price is rebuilt once however many tills ask, and keep the warm-up and all six doors.
options.verdict: Trade-off: one rebuild each, all at once
options.part2: Lucan turned it on Tuesday night. On Wednesday the warm-up ran at 5:50, I opened all six doors at 6:00, and at 6:00:00.5 every price ran out at once. 600 lookups a second missed, but the stockroom got exactly 50 rebuilds, one per price, all 50 at once, and at 6:00:01.0 every board was lit again. At 6:10:01.0 they all went dark together for half a second, then at 6:20:01.5, and every 10 minutes after that, a little later each time. Each time the stockroom took all 50 at once, as many as it can work on at full speed, while 600 lookups a second waited. At 11:40 Lucan's deploy emptied the cache, and it was the same: half a second of dark, then light. Every ten minutes, all day, the whole crowd stopped and looked up at the boards together, then went back to shopping.
options.senior: Coalescing caps every herd at one rebuild per price, and here that was enough to keep the store open. It doesn't stop prices that went in together from running out together, so the whole set lands on the stockroom at once every 10 minutes, right at its limit, and every board blinks. With 60 prices it would have been past the 50 it works on at full speed, and with several price servers each one coalesces only its own lookups. Add jitter, and warm the cache and open the doors gradually so the first fill isn't one burst.

sim.title: Run the doors at Brackwater's
sim.lede: You're Lucan, replaying a sale morning at Brackwater's from 05:59:57. At 6:00 the bell rings and the doors open. Each open door brings 100 lookups a second, spread evenly over the 50 sale prices, so all six bring 600, 12 for each price. The price service does cache-aside: a fresh price in the cache answers at once, and a miss asks the stockroom to rebuild the price. The stockroom works on 50 rebuilds at once at full speed, half a second each, so it manages 100 a second; with more in progress it shares its time, and every rebuild in progress slows down together. A till waits 2 seconds, then gives up, and a rebuild that comes back after that is thrown away, so it never reaches the cache. Lucan's warm-up puts all 50 prices in at 05:50:00.5. With jitter, the sim spreads the random extras evenly on purpose: price 1 gets a point somewhere in the first 2.4 seconds, price 2 in the next 2.4, and so on, so no more than 2 prices run out in any second. Real jitter is plain random, and now and then a few land together. Serve stale keeps a price up to a minute past its TTL while one lookup refreshes it. Rebuilds per price counts the rebuilds since the bell, the skip or the last restart, divided by the prices they were for. Changing a setting replays the morning. The clock runs twice as fast as real life. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press nothing and watch Monday: every board dark, the stockroom asked for 600 rebuilds a second, the first tills giving up at 06:00:02 and 6,000 rebuilds in progress by 06:00:10, with none answered. Turn on coalescing: 50 rebuilds, and every board lit half a second after the bell. Turn it off and open one door every 10 seconds instead: lit in 0.9 seconds, one rebuild per price. Now pick Lucan's warm-up with all six doors: lit at the bell, dark at 06:00:00.5. Add coalescing, then try serve stale instead, then jitter, and read the summary line each time. Last, with one door at a time and the warm-up, skip to 06:09:55 and watch 06:10:01. Then turn on coalescing (the morning replays), skip again, watch 06:10:01 and press Deploy.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the walls froze the store. On Monday an empty cache, and on Tuesday a cache whose 50 prices all ran out in the same half second, turned 600 lookups a second into 600 rebuilds a second for a stockroom that manages 100. That's a cache stampede, and at full load it feeds itself.

steps.title: A thundering herd is everyone at once.
steps.text: A thundering herd is many clients doing the same thing at the same moment. At Brackwater's the bell did it: six doors opened together, and 600 lookups a second arrived in the same instant. Herds form wherever something lines clients up: a sale that starts on the hour, a deploy that restarts every server, retries that all wait the same time, keys that all expire together. A herd is harmless while the cache answers. It becomes a problem the moment the cache can't, because then every client asks the slow thing behind it at once.

steps.title: A cache stampede feeds itself.
steps.text: A cache stampede, or dogpile, is a herd meeting a missing key. In cache-aside every lookup that misses asks the database to rebuild the value, and nothing stops many lookups rebuilding the same one. How many pile up is the request rate times the rebuild time: 12 lookups a second for one price, times half a second, is 6 rebuilds of that price even while the stockroom keeps up. Monday's cache was cold, its hit ratio 0, so all 600 lookups a second became rebuilds, six times the 100 the stockroom manages. A busy database doesn't just make work wait its turn: the rebuilds in progress share its CPU and disk, so each one slows down. By 6:00:10 there were 6,000 in progress and none had finished. In cache-aside it's the price service that writes the answer back, and it had given up after 2 seconds, so nothing reached the cache, the hit ratio stayed at 0, and the stockroom spent the morning on wasted work: answers nobody was waiting for. At full load a stampede doesn't recover on its own: something has to cut the load or the rebuilds, which is why Lucan had to restart the stockroom and the doorman had to empty the store.

steps.title: One rebuild per key: coalescing, locks and leases.
steps.text: Request coalescing, or single flight, lets the first miss for a key rebuild it and makes later misses wait for that answer. Monday with coalescing is 50 rebuilds instead of 600 a second, all inside the stockroom's full speed, and every board lit half a second after the bell. Inside one program it's a few lines, such as Go's singleflight package. Across many servers the shared cache has to choose who rebuilds: a lock on the key, or a lease, the token Facebook's memcache gives one client to refill a key while it tells the rest to wait and ask again. Proxies do it too: nginx's proxy_cache_lock lets one request fill a new cache entry while the others wait. The cost: everyone waiting rides on one rebuild, so it needs its own timeout, and a lock needs a plan for a holder that dies. And it limits rebuilds per key, not the number of keys: a cache of 50,000 items that comes back empty still means 50,000 rebuilds.

steps.title: Keys that go in together run out together.
steps.text: Tuesday's cache was warm, and it went dark anyway. Lucan's warm-up put all 50 prices in at 05:50:00.5, each for exactly 10 minutes, so all 50 ran out at 06:00:00.5, half a second after the bell: a synchronized expiry, a cold cache on a timer. Three fixes help. Jitter adds a random extra to each TTL, here 0 to 2 minutes, so the prices run out one or two at a time and the stockroom rebuilds one or two prices at once instead of all 50. Serving stale while one refreshes hands out the old price for a short while and lets one lookup fetch the new one, which HTTP calls stale-while-revalidate: no board goes dark, but it can't help an empty cache. And refreshing early lets a request rebuild a hot key a little before it expires, an idea called probabilistic early expiration, which a 2015 paper studied and made optimal.

steps.title: Warm first, then let them in a few at a time.
steps.text: A cache that starts empty has to be filled before the crowd arrives, or slowly while it does. Warming means loading the hot keys before taking traffic: Lucan's warm-up, or Facebook letting an empty cluster read from a full one. Letting traffic in gradually means the misses arrive no faster than the database can rebuild them. That's Rule 7. One door brings 100 lookups a second, so the 50 prices are rebuilt one each, never more than 50 in progress, all at full speed, and every board is lit in 0.9 seconds. Every door after that finds a warm cache. Deploys deserve the same care: restart cache nodes and servers a few at a time, a rolling restart, and warm each one before it takes traffic, and never empty the whole fleet's cache at the bell.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Wednesday from 6:00 to 6:02. The doors open one every 10 seconds and reach 600 lookups a second by 6:00:50. The warm-up script filled all 50 prices at 5:50. The price service sends one rebuild per price. The price cache holds 50 of 50 prices, each for 10 minutes plus a random 0 to 2 minutes, and answers nearly every lookup. The stockroom database, 50 at once at full speed, never has more than 2 rebuilds in progress.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Wednesday from 6:00 to 6:02. The warm-up filled the 50 prices at 5:50, each with its own random extra of up to 2 minutes. The doors opened one every 10 seconds, 600 lookups a second by 6:00:50, nearly all hits. When a price ran out, the price service sent one rebuild for it however many tills asked: 50 rebuilds in two minutes, never more than 2 at once.

fix.title: The fix: warm the cache, rebuild each price once, spread the expiries, and open the doors a few at a time
fix.text: Run the warm-up before the bell, and give every price its own random extra on the TTL, 0 to 2 minutes here, so the 50 prices never run out in the same second. Turn on coalescing so one lookup rebuilds each missing price and the others wait for it; with several price servers, use a lock or lease in the external cache so it's one rebuild per price in total. Where a slightly old price is fine, serve it for up to a minute while one lookup refreshes it. Open one door every 10 seconds: one door's 100 lookups a second rebuild all 50 prices without the stockroom ever going past the 50 it works on at full speed, and every door after that finds a warm cache. Make deploys behave the same way: restart cache nodes one at a time and warm the hot keys before a node takes traffic. Then watch the stockroom's load at the bell and after every deploy, and the rebuilds per price.

limits: Coalescing and leases limit rebuilds per key, not the number of keys. A cache of 50,000 items that comes back empty still sends 50,000 different rebuilds, so a cold start at scale still needs warming and a gradual start, and everyone waiting on a key shares the fate of its one rebuild. Give the database a timeout no longer than the till's 2 seconds, or cancel the rebuild when the till gives up, so it stops doing wasted work.

Serving stale and jittered TTLs both mean some answers are older than before. That's fine for a price board for a minute, not for anything you charge or promise: the till should still check the source of truth at payment.

Letting traffic in a few at a time only works where you control the doors. Shoppers on a website arrive when they like: there the same idea is a waiting room or a gradual shift of traffic, and the cache has to survive a full crowd on its own.

Answers up to the stale window out of date, a minute here.

explain.seniorTake: When many requests can arrive at the same moment, plan for the moment the cache can't answer them: the opening bell, a deploy, a restart, a batch of keys running out together. An empty cache has a hit ratio of 0, so every request becomes a rebuild, and past the database's limit every rebuild slows the others until none finishes before its caller gives up and the cache never fills. So let traffic in a few at a time while the cache fills, warm the hot keys before you open, rebuild each key once with coalescing or a lease, spread expiries with jitter, and serve slightly stale data while one request refreshes it. Then measure: the database's load at opening and after every deploy, rebuilds per key, and how long until the hit ratio is back.

realWorld.title: Facebook's leases
realWorld.text: In Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013), Rajesh Nishtala and colleagues introduce leases to address two problems, stale sets and thundering herds. In their paper a thundering herd happens when a specific key undergoes heavy read and write activity: writes keep invalidating the recently set value, so many reads take the more costly path to the database. On a miss, a memcached server gives the client a lease, a 64-bit token bound to that key, and the client presents it when it puts the value back. To calm the herd, each server hands out a token only once every 10 seconds per key; other requests in those 10 seconds are told to wait a short time, and typically the client with the lease has set the data within a few milliseconds. For a week of misses on keys particularly prone to thundering herds, the peak database query rate was 17K/s without leases and 1.3K/s with them. Facebook provisions its databases for peak load, so the paper calls that a significant efficiency gain.

realWorld.title: Stale values at Facebook
realWorld.text: The same paper lets some reads skip the wait. When a key is deleted, its value moves to a structure of recently deleted items for a short time, and a get can return either a lease token or data marked as stale. Applications that can make progress with slightly out-of-date data don't wait for the database, and the paper reports that most applications can use a stale value without any changes.

realWorld.title: Facebook's Cold Cluster Warmup
realWorld.text: When Facebook brings a new cluster online, an existing one fails, or it performs scheduled maintenance, the caches have very poor hit rates. A system called Cold Cluster Warmup lets clients in the cold cluster, the frontend cluster with an empty cache, fetch data from a warm cluster's caches instead of persistent storage, which brings cold clusters back to full capacity in a few hours instead of a few days. To avoid filling the cold cluster with a value that has just changed, deletes there carry a two-second hold-off time that rejects adds of that key, and the system is turned off once the cold cluster's hit rate stabilizes.

realWorld.title: Gutter: a small stampede, caught
realWorld.text: When a memcached server stops answering, every request for its keys would fall through to the database. Facebook dedicates a small pool of machines called Gutter, about 1% of a cluster's memcached servers, to take over for a few failed servers, and entries there expire quickly. The paper says this reduces the rate of client-visible failures by 99% and converts 10% to 25% of failures into hits each day, and when a server fails entirely, Gutter's hit rates generally exceed 35% in under 4 minutes.

realWorld.title: AWS on cold starts and herds
realWorld.text: In Amazon's article Caching challenges and strategies, first published in the Builders' Library, its authors warn that in-memory caches suffer cold starts: a new server launches with a completely empty cache, which can cause a burst of requests to the dependent service as it fills, a significant issue during deployments or whenever the cache is flushed fleet-wide. They describe the thundering herd as many clients making requests that need the same uncached downstream resource at about the same time, which can lead to throttling or brownout. Their remedy is request coalescing, where the servers or an external cache make sure only one pending request is out for an uncached resource, and they note that some caching libraries, and caches such as Nginx and Varnish, support it.

realWorld.title: The stampede, measured
realWorld.text: Andrea Vattani, Flavio Chierichetti and Keegan Lowenstein's VLDB 2015 paper, Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention, describes a cache stampede, also called dog-piling, cache miss storm or cache choking, as a popular cache item expiring and many requests seeing the miss and regenerating it at the same time. Their example: an item read 10 times a second that takes 3 seconds to recompute is recomputed by 30 requests. They add that concurrent recomputations slow each other down by bogging down the system, pulling still more requests into the stampede, which is why it's often called a cascading failure. They compare three fixes: a separate process that recomputes items, locking, and probabilistic early expiration, where each request may refresh the item a little before it expires, with the chance rising as expiry nears. Locking leaves the other requests with nothing to return unless they wait or use a stale item, needs a time to live for the lock itself, and isn't fault-tolerant if the request holding the lock fails. Their algorithm, XFetch, uses an exponential distribution, which they show to be optimal.

realWorld.title: stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error
realWorld.text: RFC 5861, HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content (Mark Nottingham, May 2010), is an Informational RFC from the Independent Submission stream, not an Internet standard. It defines stale-while-revalidate, which lets a cache return a stale response at once while it revalidates in the background, hiding latency from clients, and stale-if-error, which lets a cache return a stale response instead of an error, meaning a 500, 502, 503 or 504. Its example, Cache-Control: max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=30, is fresh for 600 seconds and may be served stale for up to 30 more while a validation is attempted. It warns that if the window is too small, or traffic too sparse, some requests fall outside it and block until the server can validate the cached response.

realWorld.title: nginx's cache lock and stale updates
realWorld.text: nginx's proxy module has both fixes. proxy_cache_lock, off by default and available since version 1.1.12, lets only one request at a time populate a new cache element; the others wait for it, up to proxy_cache_lock_timeout, 5 seconds by default, after which a request is passed to the proxied server and its response isn't cached. proxy_cache_use_stale with the updating parameter serves a stale cached response while it's being updated, which the documentation says minimizes the number of accesses to proxied servers, and proxy_cache_background_update, since version 1.11.10, refreshes an expired item in a background subrequest while the stale response is returned.

realWorld.title: Go's singleflight
realWorld.text: Go's golang.org/x/sync (the version pkg.go.dev showed when this case was written was v0.24.0) includes the singleflight package, which its documentation describes as a way to suppress duplicate calls. Its Do call runs the work for a key, making sure that only one run is in flight for a given key at a time; if a duplicate call comes in, it waits for the original to complete and receives the same results. That's request coalescing inside one program. It doesn't coordinate separate servers.

realWorld.title: Jitter on TTLs
realWorld.text: Amazon ElastiCache's best-practices page for semantic caching, where a cache keeps the answers of large language models, sets each entry's TTL with random jitter to spread out cache invalidations: a base of 82,800 seconds, about 23 hours, plus a random 0 to 3,600 seconds. The same idea fits any cache whose keys tend to be written together.

asked: What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?
You deploy, and the database falls over. Why?
interview.answer: A cache stampede is a thundering herd hitting a missing key: when a hot key expires, or the whole cache is cold after a deploy or restart, every request misses at once and each one asks the database to rebuild the same value. Past the database's limit the rebuilds slow each other, requests time out before the value is written back, the hit ratio stays at 0, and the database falls over. That's why a deploy that restarts every cache node, or every app server holding an in-memory cache, can take the database down. Prevent it in layers. Request coalescing, or single flight, lets one request rebuild each key while the others wait for its result; across servers, use a lock or a lease in the shared cache, as Facebook's memcache does. Serve the stale value while one request refreshes it. Add jitter to TTLs so keys written together don't expire together, or refresh hot keys a little early. Warm the hot keys before taking traffic, restart a few nodes at a time, and let traffic in gradually. Then say what you'd watch: the database's load and the hit ratio during deploys, and rebuilds per key. You'll build a stampede scenario, a cache that restarts at peak with an option for request coalescing, into your own simulator in Loadout's Build Night L2.

terms.def: A large shop selling many kinds of goods on several floors, from coats to kitchenware. Brackwater's has six doors onto the street.
A rebuild of a shop's fittings. Brackwater's refit put in new tills, price boards and the price service, which started with an empty cache.
A screen above a rail that shows an item's price. At Brackwater's it asks the price service for the price, and goes dark when it can't get one.
A scanner on a pillar where shoppers check a price. It asks the price service, like a till or a board.
One request for one sale price, from a till, board or price checker. Each open door's crowd brings 100 a second; all six bring 600.
Brackwater's program that answers every lookup. It does cache-aside: it looks in the price cache first, and on a miss asks the stockroom to rebuild the price.
The price service's cache: the 50 sale prices kept in memory, each for 10 minutes on Monday and Tuesday.
Brackwater's database of items, sale rules and stock. It works on 50 rebuilds at once at full speed, half a second each: 100 a second. Past 50 it shares its time.
Fetching a missing value again from the slow source: here, the stockroom finding the item, applying the sale and counting the stock to make a price.
Started but not finished. The stockroom's count of rebuilds in progress includes ones whose till has already given up.
A till waits 2 seconds for a price. After that it stops waiting and its board stays dark, but the stockroom keeps working on the rebuild.
Work a server finishes after its caller has gone. The database can't tell that the client left, so it keeps answering nobody.
The bell rung at 6:00 when Brackwater's opens its doors on a sale morning.
A person employed to open a building's doors and manage who comes in.
A uniform worn by a household's or a business's staff. Brackwater's old doormen wore grey livery.
Filling a cache with its hot keys before traffic arrives. Lucan's warm-up runs at 5:50 and asks for all 50 sale prices.
A cache already holding its hot keys, so most lookups are hits.
An empty cache, after a start, restart, refit or deploy. Its hit ratio is 0, so every lookup misses until it fills.
A key that gets far more requests than most, like a sale price on opening morning.
Many clients doing the same thing at the same moment, such as a crowd at an opening bell, servers restarting together or keys expiring together, so a shared resource gets them all at once.
A herd meeting a missing key: every request for it misses at once and each asks the database to rebuild the same value. Also called a dogpile.
Another name for a cache stampede.
Letting the first miss for a key rebuild it while later misses for the same key wait for that one answer. Also called single flight.
Another name for request coalescing: only one rebuild of a key in flight at a time.
Sent and not yet finished, like a rebuild the stockroom is still working on.
A programming language made at Google, often used for servers.
A unit of Go code that other programs can use, such as singleflight.
A Go package that suppresses duplicate calls: one call per key runs, and duplicates wait for it and get the same result.
A collection of extra Go packages for running work at the same time, kept by the Go project but shipped separately from the language itself. singleflight is one of them.
A marker in a shared cache saying one client is rebuilding a key, so the others wait or use an old value. It needs a timeout in case the holder dies.
In Facebook's memcache, a 64-bit token a cache server gives one client on a miss, letting it put the value back. Other clients are told to wait and ask again.
Facebook's term for a web server writing a value into the cache that is no longer the latest one, because updates arrived out of order.
Storage that keeps data when the power is off, such as a database on disk.
In Facebook's paper, a group of web servers and memcached servers that serve users together.
Facebook's names for a frontend cluster whose caches are empty (cold) and one whose caches have normal hit rates (warm).
Facebook's system that lets a cold cluster's clients read from a warm cluster's caches instead of the database while the cold one fills.
A short time after a delete during which a cache refuses to add the key back. Facebook uses two seconds in its cold clusters.
Facebook's small pool of spare memcached servers, about 1% of a cluster, that takes over the keys of a few failed servers so their misses don't all reach the database.
When a cached value runs out, handing out the old one for a short while and letting one request fetch the new one. Deliberate, unlike DNS serve-stale, a fallback for when the source is down.
The HTTP Cache-Control extension from RFC 5861 that lets a cache serve a stale response for a set number of seconds while it revalidates in the background.
The RFC 5861 extension that lets a cache serve a stale response instead of an error such as a 500, 502, 503 or 504.
To check with the server a cached copy came from whether it's still good, or fetch a new one.
Done without making the request that triggered it wait, like a refresh that runs while the old price is handed out.
The HTTP header that tells caches whether and how long a response may be kept, with settings such as max-age.
A Cache-Control setting: how many seconds a response stays fresh.
Status codes a proxy returns when the server behind it sent a bad answer (502) or no answer in time (504).
A TTL with a random extra added for each key, so keys written together don't expire together. The same idea as jitter on retry waits, moved to the expiry.
Many keys expiring at the same moment because they were written together with the same TTL, or given the same expiry time.
Letting each request rebuild a key a little before it expires, with a chance that rises as expiry nears, so one request usually refreshes it before the herd arrives.
The probabilistic early expiration algorithm from the 2015 VLDB paper, which picks how early to refresh using an exponential distribution.
A way of drawing random amounts where small ones are common and large ones are rare.
A failure that spreads: an overloaded part slows down, which makes the work waiting on it pile up and adds still more load.
Very Large Data Bases, a research conference on databases. The stampede paper appeared in its 2015 proceedings.
An RFC published to share information, not to set an Internet standard.
An RFC published by the RFC Editor directly, outside the usual standards process.
An nginx setting that lets one request at a time fill a new cache entry while the others wait. Off by default.
How long requests wait on proxy_cache_lock. After it, a request goes to the server and its response isn't cached. 5 seconds by default.
An nginx setting listing when a stale cached response may be served. Its updating parameter serves stale while the entry is being refreshed.
An nginx setting that refreshes an expired cache entry in a background subrequest while the stale response is returned.
A request a server makes internally, on its own behalf, while it handles another.
The server behind a proxy, which the proxy forwards requests to.
An open-source caching proxy that sits in front of web servers.
A partial outage: a service still answers, but slowly or with some errors.
Deliberately turning some requests away so the rest can still be served.
A service yours calls and waits on, such as a database. Load you send it travels downstream.
Further along the chain of calls: a database is downstream of the service that queries it.
A cache that runs outside the app's own servers, such as Redis on ElastiCache, shared by all of them.
One cache that every server reads and writes, such as Redis, so a price one till fetched is there for all the others. Another name for an external cache.
Happening at the same time, like many rebuilds of the same price running together.
Able to keep working correctly when one part fails.
Amazon's collection of articles by its engineers on how Amazon builds and runs services.
To set up capacity in advance. Facebook sizes its databases for peak load.
Caching the answers to questions so that similar questions, not only identical ones, can reuse them. Often used with large language models.
An AI model trained on large amounts of text that answers by writing text, such as the model behind a chatbot.
Restarting servers or cache nodes a few at a time, so most keep serving with warm caches while the others refill.
A written list of steps for a routine or emergency operation, such as a safe deploy.
When the doors open at 6 AM, let them in a few at a time: let traffic in gradually while a cache fills, so misses arrive no faster than the database can rebuild them.
A CloudWatch metric for an Amazon RDS database: the percentage of its CPU in use.
A CloudWatch metric for an Amazon RDS database: the number of client network connections to it.

atWork: Pick a service your team runs behind a cache: ElastiCache, an in-memory cache inside the app, or a CDN. Read-only access is enough. Open its deploy history: does a deploy restart every cache node, or every app server holding an in-memory cache, at the same moment? In CloudWatch, chart CacheHitRate (or your own hit ratio) beside the database's CPUUtilization and DatabaseConnections around the last deploy. A hit ratio that drops toward 0 while the database's load jumps is a cold-cache stampede, even if it recovered. Then search the code for how TTLs are set: is every key given the same fixed TTL, or the same expiry time, such as midnight? Does anything coalesce misses, such as Go's singleflight, a lock in Redis or nginx's proxy_cache_lock? If not, draft the runbook fix: restart cache nodes one at a time, warm the hottest keys before a node takes traffic, add jitter to TTLs, and turn on coalescing.

recall.prompt: Your team deploys the product service at 2 PM. The deploy restarts all 8 app servers at once, and each one keeps product pages in an in-memory cache. Within a minute the database is at 100% CPU, pages time out, and nothing gets better until someone scales the database up. What happened, and what do you change in the deploy and in the code?

keyIdeas.idea: Every server came back with an empty cache, so every request missed at once: a cold-cache stampede
Past its limit the database slows every query, requests give up before results are written back, so the cache never fills and it can't recover alone
Restart servers a few at a time and warm the hot keys before each one takes traffic
Coalesce misses (single flight, a lock or a lease) so each key is rebuilt once, and add jitter to TTLs

recall.model: Each server came back from the deploy with an empty in-memory cache, so its hit ratio was 0 and every request went to the database at once: a cold-cache stampede, eight servers' worth. Past its limit the database slows every query, so requests time out before their results are written back, the caches never fill, and it can't recover until the load drops or the database grows. In the deploy: restart a few servers at a time, and warm each one's hottest keys before it takes traffic. In the code: coalesce misses so each key is rebuilt once per server, or once in total with a lock or lease in a shared cache; add jitter to TTLs so keys written together don't expire together; and watch the database's load and the hit ratio during every deploy.

recall.prompt: A price is looked up 12 times a second, and rebuilding it takes half a second while the database keeps up. Its cached copy expires, and there's no coalescing. About how many rebuilds of that price start before the first one finishes?
recall.why: Every lookup in the half second before the first rebuild finishes misses too: 12 a second times 0.5 s is 6. The VLDB paper's example is the same sum, 10 a second for 3 seconds making 30. With coalescing it's 1, and if the database is overloaded so each rebuild slows down, it's many more.

recall.prompt: Which fix does nothing for a cache that has just restarted empty?
options: Serving stale while one request refreshes
Warming the hot keys before it takes traffic
recall.why: Serving stale needs an old copy to hand out, and an empty cache has none. Coalescing still cuts each key to one rebuild, warming fills the cache before traffic, and letting traffic in gradually keeps the misses within what the database can rebuild.

recall.prompt: A teammate warms the cache at 08:55 with every key set to expire in exactly one hour, so it's full for the 9 AM rush. Every day at about 9:55 the database spikes and pages slow down for a few seconds. What's happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Every key went in at once with the same TTL, so they all expire at the same moment
Add a random extra to each TTL (jitter) so expiries spread out
Rebuild each key once with coalescing, or serve the stale value while one request refreshes, or refresh hot keys early

recall.model: The warm-up wrote every key in the same moment with the same one-hour TTL, so at 9:55 they all expire together and every request for them misses at once: a stampede on a timer, with the morning's traffic already there. Add jitter: give each key a random extra of a few minutes, so expiries spread out and only a few keys are rebuilt at a time. Coalesce misses so each key is rebuilt once, and for data that may be slightly old, serve the stale value while one request refreshes it, or refresh hot keys a little before they expire.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Brackwater's opened an online shop for the spring sale, which starts at 9 PM on Friday. Lucan now runs the price service on 4 servers, each with coalescing, all reading one shared price cache. At 8:58 he shipped a fix, and his script restarted every cache node at once. At 9:00:00, 20,000 people pressed refresh. The stockroom got 4 rebuilds of every price, one from each server, and every phone tried again each second its page failed. The website was down until 9:14. At the store, the doors opened one at a time, as they do now.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the website fall over when the store didn't, and what should Lucan change?

keyIdeas.idea: The restart emptied the whole cache just before the peak: a cold-cache stampede
Restart cache nodes one by one, not right before a sale, and warm the hot prices first
Coalescing works inside each server, so 4 servers still mean 4 rebuilds: use a lock or lease in the shared cache for one in total
Phones retrying every second are a herd of their own: back off with jitter, and let shoppers in gradually with a waiting room

coldCase.model: The store survived because its traffic arrives through doors Lucan controls. The website's doesn't: at 9:00, 20,000 people arrived at once, and Lucan's 8:58 restart had just emptied every cache node, so the hit ratio was 0 and every request was a rebuild. Coalescing helped less than he hoped because it works inside each server: 4 servers meant 4 rebuilds of every price. And each failed page made the phones try again every second, a herd of retries on top. Restart cache nodes one by one, never minutes before a sale, and warm the hot prices before each node takes traffic. Put a lock or lease in the shared cache so one server rebuilds each price in total. Make the phones back off with jitter instead of retrying every second. And do online what the doors do: a waiting room that lets shoppers in a few at a time.

next: Next, Mirrors Everywhere: a touring band's fan site that loads in a blink in every city on the tour, from copies kept near each one, and in one city still shows a concert the band cancelled a week ago.

sources.title: Rajesh Nishtala et al., Scaling Memcache at Facebook, 10th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI '13), 2013 (section 3.2.1 leases for stale sets and thundering herds: a 64-bit token per key, a token only once every 10 seconds per key, peak database query rate 17K/s without leases and 1.3K/s with them; stale values; section 3.3 Gutter, about 1% of servers, 99% fewer client-visible failures, 10% to 25% of failures converted into hits, over 35% hit rates in under 4 minutes; section 4.3 Cold Cluster Warmup, a few hours instead of a few days, two-second hold-off)

RFC 5861, HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content (M. Nottingham, Informational, Independent Submission, May 2010): stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error, with the max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=30 example

Andrea Vattani, Flavio Chierichetti and Keegan Lowenstein, Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention, Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, Vol. 8, No. 8, 2015 (cache stampede, dog-piling, cache miss storm, cache choking; 10 requests a second times 3 seconds is 30 recomputations; external recomputation, locking and probabilistic early expiration; XFetch)

Go packages: golang.org/x/sync/singleflight, page as shown for v0.24.0 (a duplicate function call suppression mechanism; Group.Do runs one execution per key, duplicates wait and receive the same results)

AWS Builder Center (formerly the Amazon Builders' Library): Caching challenges and strategies, by Jas Chhabra, first published with Matt Brinkley (cold starts during deployments; the thundering herd; request coalescing; Nginx and Varnish; load shedding and capping requests to dependent services)

nginx documentation: Module ngx_http_proxy_module (proxy_cache_lock, off by default, since 1.1.12; proxy_cache_lock_timeout 5s; proxy_cache_use_stale updating; proxy_cache_background_update, since 1.11.10)

Amazon ElastiCache User Guide: Semantic caching best practices (setting cache invalidation periods: a TTL of 82,800 seconds plus random jitter of up to 3,600 seconds to spread out cache invalidations)

Amazon RDS User Guide: Amazon CloudWatch metrics for Amazon RDS (CPUUtilization, the percentage of CPU utilization; DatabaseConnections, the number of client network connections to the database instance)
Amazon ElastiCache User Guide: Metrics for Valkey and Redis OSS (CacheHitRate)
